analysis.time: The report is based on data up to week 45 of 2026 (2 November to 8 November 2026).
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers England, focusing on influenza and other seasonal respiratory viruses in the population.
analysis.event: The report indicates that influenza activity increased and is circulating at low levels, with ED attendances for influenza-like-illness above seasonally expected levels. It also notes that influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection incidents increased compared with the previous week.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Emergency department attendances for influenza-like-illness were above seasonally expected levels, and the number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection incidents increased compared with the previous week. analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 12 November 2026 (week 46) highlights that influenza activity in England has increased and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department attendances for influenza-like-illness (ILI) have risen above seasonally expected levels, and the number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents has increased compared to the previous week. The report also notes that vaccine uptake among certain groups, such as those aged 65 and over, is lower than the previous season. While influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) to the Mean Standard Deviation Method (MSD), data for weeks 41 and 42 was incomplete, but this has been corrected since week 43. The report emphasizes that the methods used for defining activity levels are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Additionally, it mentions that the Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS) captures test results for influenza and other respiratory viruses, and the unified sample dataset (USD) is used to calculate positivity rates for SARS-CoV-2. Overall, the report provides an updated overview of influenza and related respiratory virus activity in England, with a focus on monitoring and data collection methods.

title: Hospitalized influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 isolates in Shiraz lack major antiviral resistance mutations

analysis.time: The study was conducted between November 2023 and December 2024, with the report published on November 15, 2026 (N1).
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on hospitalized patients in Shiraz, Iran, with a total of 300 respiratory samples collected (N9).
analysis.event: An observational study investigated influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 isolates from hospitalized patients in Shiraz, Iran, between November 2023 and December 2024, revealing genomic variability but no major antiviral resistance mutations (N1).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study identified 14 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 isolates from 300 samples, with 18 distinct amino acid substitutions across the neuraminidase gene. None of the isolates carried major resistance markers like H275Y or I223V (N11, N16, N22).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study involved full-length neuraminidase gene sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, structural modeling, and molecular docking to assess antiviral susceptibility. The findings suggest that standard antiviral therapies remain effective against the analyzed isolates (N12, N13, N24).

analysis.brief_en: A study conducted between November 2023 and December 2024 in Shiraz, Iran, analyzed influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 isolates from hospitalized patients. Researchers collected 300 respiratory samples and identified 14 positive cases for further molecular analysis. The investigation revealed multiple amino acid substitutions in the neuraminidase gene, including V241I and N369K, which were prevalent in 92.9% of isolates. However, none of the isolates carried major resistance markers such as H275Y or I223V, which are known to reduce susceptibility to antiviral drugs like oseltamivir and zanamivir. The study also performed structural modeling and molecular docking to confirm that the analyzed variants maintain predicted binding to these therapeutic agents. These findings suggest that standard antiviral treatments remain effective against the circulating influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 strains in Shiraz during the study period. The research highlights the importance of continuous molecular surveillance to monitor potential changes in viral properties that could affect drug efficacy.

title: Single amino acid change broadens influenza B mRNA vaccine protection

analysis.time: The study was published on November 14, 2026, and the research was conducted with experiments carried out 35 days after booster immunization. The findings were based on data collected up to 14 days post-challenge.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted in Beijing, China, involving female BALB/c mice as the experimental population. The study also references global influenza B strains from the GISAID database.
analysis.event: Researchers at the National Institutes for Drug Control in Beijing demonstrated that a single amino acid substitution (D212N) in the hemagglutinin protein of an influenza B vaccine candidate significantly broadens its protective capacity in mice. This modification was shown to enhance cross-neutralizing antibody responses against diverse subclades of the B/Victoria lineage.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study highlights a potential improvement in vaccine efficacy against the B/Victoria lineage, with the D212N-modified vaccine showing 100% survival in challenge experiments. The WHO-recommended BV21 strain lacks a glycosylation position that is associated with broader cross-protection, which this modification addresses.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted using an mRNA platform and tested in mice. analysis.event: Flu test positivity exceeded 10% nationally, with influenza A (H1N1pdm09 and H3N2) and influenza B (Victoria and Yamagata lineages) being the dominant viruses. The CDC reported increased activity and hospitalizations, with a preliminary assessment of low severity.

analysis.time: The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) urges Georgians to get vaccinated against the flu now. analysis.location_and_population: Everyone over the age of six months should get a flu vaccine, with rare exceptions.
analysis.event: The single most effective way to prevent the flu is the flu vaccine. Flu is a potentially serious disease, especially for young children and older adults, that can lead to hospitalization and sometimes even death.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: All 2026–2027 seasonal influenza vaccines are trivalent, meaning they protect against three flu strains: influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B/Victoria virus. Flu symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, headache, chills, and fatigue. One of the most pronounced flu symptoms is a sudden onset of achiness and malaise.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: There are other tried and true measures you can take to help prevent the spread of flu and other respiratory diseases, including: Wash your hands frequently and thoroughly with soap and warm water. title: Pediatric Inpatient Influenza Detections Correlated Positively With Southern China Regional Surveillance

analysis.time: The study was conducted over a 65-month period, with the publication date on November 15, 2026. The data collection spanned from January 2021 to May 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on pediatric inpatients in southern China, specifically children aged 0 to 14 years who presented with lower respiratory tract infections.
analysis.event: A retrospective analysis of pediatric inpatient influenza testing records showed that the monthly shares of influenza types and subtypes were positively correlated with regional surveillance data from the Chinese National Influenza Center. The study also found that within each calendar year, the same leading influenza category was identified through both hospital-based detections and regional surveillance.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study reported test positivity rates of 2.51% for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, 3.34% for influenza A(H3N2), and 2.18% for influenza B. The findings indicate that routine inpatient testing can effectively supplement regional influenza surveillance by providing localized, age-stratified detection data.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was a retrospective analysis using molecular testing records and statistical models. It demonstrated strong positive correlations between hospital-based influenza detections and regional surveillance data, with 79.5% agreement in identifying the leading category in 44 months. The authors concluded that routine inpatient testing can effectively supplement regional influenza surveillance.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 15, 2026, analyzed 21,965 throat-swab testing records from pediatric and neonatal inpatients in southern China between January 2021 and May 2026. The research found that monthly shares of influenza types and subtypes, including A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B, were positively correlated with regional surveillance data from the Chinese National Influenza Center. Within each calendar year, the same leading influenza category was consistently identified through both hospital-based detections and regional surveillance. The study also revealed that children aged 6 to 14 years had higher adjusted odds ratios for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B compared to infants under 1 year. The authors concluded that routine inpatient testing can effectively supplement regional influenza surveillance by providing localized, age-stratified detection data. The findings highlight the potential of hospital-based molecular testing to align with broader epidemiological trends, offering insights into seasonal influenza dynamics among hospitalized children.
